questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A feedback loop that a linear account cannot order
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a feedback loop that linear ordering cannot capture
questions.stem: A historian describes a revolt that strengthened the grievances that caused it.

options.text: The account is inadequate because the loop cannot be captured by a before-and-after chain.
The account is fine because it lists events in chronological order.
The account works if the historian picks a starting point.
options.misconception: thinks a starting point fixes the loop

options.text: The account is strong because it is detailed.

questions.explanation: A feedback loop runs in both directions, so a linear before-and-after chain cannot represent it. The account must show the reciprocal influence.
questions.hint: Show the reciprocal influence.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Recognising and testing a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Recognise and test a threshold in a historical case
questions.stem: A historian claims a riot became a revolution once casualties passed a certain point.

answer.exemplar: The claim posits a threshold; to test it, the historian must specify the level and check cases on both sides, since a threshold asserted without a test risks being a post-hoc label.

questions.explanation: A threshold must be specified and tested against cases on both sides. Otherwise it is a label applied after the fact.
questions.hint: Specify and test the threshold.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Telling a necessary condition from a sufficient one
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions

stimulus.body: The case note lists three factors present in every successful revolt, but no single factor alone produced success. The historian calls each one sufficient.

questions.stem: A historian labels each factor present in every success as sufficient.

options.text: The label is correct because presence in all successes implies sufficiency.
The label is fine if the factors are combined.
The label is wrong because presence in all successes implies necessity, not sufficiency.
The label is acceptable in a preliminary draft.

questions.explanation: A factor present in every success is necessary, not sufficient. Sufficiency requires that the factor alone produces success.
questions.hint: Present in all successes means necessary.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A condition present in every success and sufficient for none
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a necessary-but-not-sufficient condition
questions.stem: A factor appears in every successful case but never produces success alone.

options.text: The factor is sufficient because it is always present.
The factor is both necessary and sufficient.
The factor is irrelevant because it never acts alone.
The factor is necessary but not sufficient for success.

questions.explanation: A factor present in every success but never sufficient alone is necessary but not sufficient. Both roles must be kept distinct.
questions.hint: Necessary does not mean sufficient.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What warrants carrying a claim past one case
questions.learningObjective: Identify the warrant for carrying a claim beyond one case
questions.stem: A historian extends a finding from one well-documented case to an entire era.

options.text: The extension needs a warrant showing the case shares the era's relevant conditions.
The extension is warranted because the case is typical.
The extension is fine if the case is famous.
The extension works if no counter-case is known.

questions.explanation: Carrying a claim past one case requires a warrant that the case shares the relevant conditions with the target. Typicality or fame is not enough.
questions.hint: Show shared relevant conditions.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.learningObjective: State the warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.stem: A historian generalises from three cases without stating why they represent the broader set.

options.text: The generalisation is acceptable because three cases are better than one.
The generalisation works if the cases are well documented.
The generalisation lacks a warrant linking the cases to the broader set.
The generalisation is fine if the historian is experienced.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The test a case chosen for its promise performs
questions.learningObjective: Understand what a promising case tests
questions.stem: A historian selects a case because it seems to promise a strong test of a theory.

answer.exemplar: A case chosen for its promise tests whether the theory holds where it should be most challenged; if the theory survives, confidence grows, and if it fails, the boundary of the theory is exposed.

questions.explanation: A promising case is selected to challenge the theory where it is most vulnerable. The outcome either strengthens or bounds the theory.
questions.hint: It challenges the theory at its weakest point.

questions.topic: What a deviant case obliges an explanation to add

questions.stem: A deviant case is handled with an ad hoc exception instead of a revised explanation.

options.text: The exception is acceptable because it preserves the theory.
The exception is fine if it is clearly labelled.
The deviant case should be excluded as an outlier.
The deviant case obliges the explanation to add a mechanism or boundary condition.

questions.subject: SEMINAR

The account is fine because it lists events in chronological order.
The account works if the historian picks a starting point.
options.misconception: thinks a starting point fixes the loop

options.text: The account is strong because it is detailed.

questions.explanation: A feedback loop runs in both directions, so a linear before-and-after chain cannot represent it. The account must show the reciprocal influence.
questions.hint: Show the reciprocal influence.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise and test a third threshold
questions.stem: A historian claims a strike became a general strike once a share of workers joined.

answer.exemplar: The claim posits a threshold; to test it, the historian must specify the level and check cases on both sides, since a threshold asserted without a test risks being a post-hoc label.

questions.explanation: A threshold must be specified and tested against cases on both sides. Otherwise it is a label applied after the fact.
questions.hint: Specify and test the threshold.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Telling a necessary condition from a sufficient one
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish necessary from sufficient in a third case

stimulus.body: The case note lists three factors present in every successful transition, but no single factor alone produced success. The historian calls each one sufficient.

questions.stem: A historian labels each factor present in every success as sufficient.

options.text: The label is correct because presence in all successes implies sufficiency.
The label is fine if the factors are combined.
The label is wrong because presence in all successes implies necessity, not sufficiency.
The label is acceptable in a preliminary draft.

questions.explanation: A factor present in every success is necessary, not sufficient. Sufficiency requires that the factor alone produces success.
questions.hint: Present in all successes means necessary.

questions.topic: A condition present in every success and sufficient for none
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a necessary-but-not-sufficient condition in a third case
questions.stem: A factor appears in every successful case but never produces success alone.

options.text: The factor is sufficient because it is always present.
The factor is both necessary and sufficient.
The factor is irrelevant because it never acts alone.
The factor is necessary but not sufficient for success.

questions.explanation: A factor present in every success but never sufficient alone is necessary but not sufficient. Both roles must be kept distinct.
questions.hint: Necessary does not mean sufficient.

options.text: The extension needs a warrant showing the case shares the region's relevant conditions.
The extension is warranted because the case is typical.
The extension is fine if the case is famous.
The extension works if no counter-case is known.

questions.explanation: Carrying a claim past one case requires a warrant that the case shares the relevant conditions with the target. Typicality or fame is not enough.

The generalisation works if the cases are well documented.

The generalisation is fine if the historian is experienced.

questions.explanation: A generalisation needs a warrant showing why the cases represent the broader set. Quantity or documentation alone does not provide it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The test a case chosen for its promise performs
questions.learningObjective: Understand a promising case in a third theory
questions.stem: A historian selects a case because it seems to promise a strong test of a theory.

answer.exemplar: A case chosen for its promise tests whether the theory holds where it should be most challenged; if the theory survives, confidence grows, and if it fails, the boundary of the theory is exposed.

questions.explanation: A promising case is selected to challenge the theory where it is most vulnerable. The outcome either strengthens or bounds the theory.
questions.hint: It challenges the theory at its weakest point.

options.text: The exception is acceptable because it preserves the theory.
The exception is fine if it is clearly labelled.
The deviant case should be excluded as an outlier.
The deviant case obliges the explanation to add a mechanism or boundary condition.

questions.explanation: A deviant case cannot be dismissed or patched with an exception. It obliges the explanation to add a mechanism or a boundary condition.

questions.explanation: Necessity requires showing that Y fails without X or under a different order. Regularity or plausibility alone does not establish it.

questions.explanation: Counts show scale and frequency; accounts show mechanism and meaning. Combining them gives a fuller picture than either alone.

answer.exemplar: Source ranking depends on the question: memoirs may be best for lived experience, while government reports may be best for policy intent; a single hierarchy misleads when the question changes.
